Body:
Adding a **variant of the same signature** on 1.18.30. It differs in the finish reason, but looks like the same loop-exit mechanism you identified.

## Signature

The assistant message persists with:

- `finish: "stop"` — **not** `unknown`
- `tokens.output = 0`
- `tokens.reasoning = 642–1819` — the model *did* generate, just not into `content`
- parts: `step-start`, `reasoning`, `step-finish` — **no `text` part**
- `step-finish` reports `{"reason":"stop","tokens":{"input":155,"output":0,"reasoning":923,"cache":{"read":406272}}}`

The `reasoning` part holds the entire answer that should have been the reply. Trimmed example of that reasoning text:

```
All cleared:
- PendingFileRenameOperations: False (cleared)
- CBS RebootPending: False (cleared)
- WU RebootRequired: False
- SET937.tmp: False (deleted)
- DPS: Running
...
So the "pending reboot" is fully resolved, ...
```

So the answer is produced and billed, but lands wholly in the reasoning channel; `content` stays empty and the turn is accepted as complete. `finish: "stop"` with no text part exits the loop exactly like `finish: "unknown"` does.

## Frequency / environment

- opencode **1.18.30**, Windows 11, provider `deepseek` (`deepseek-flash`), thinking enabled, `@ai-sdk/openai-compatible` path.
- **10 occurrences in one day**, all in a single session (17:12 → 22:10 local). Each 5.3–10.1 s wall clock, `reasoning` 642–1819, `output` always 0.
- No `level=ERROR`, no `cancel`, no retry. The log goes `stream` → `loop step=N` → `exiting loop`. Nothing is surfaced; the session just goes idle mid-task.

Context size is **not** a discriminator: affected turns had `cache.read` 244K–430K, while normal completions in the same DB average 265K (max 438K) — the ranges overlap completely.

## Two hypotheses already falsified, so nobody repeats them

- Removing `interleaved: { field: "reasoning_content" }` from the model config — **no effect**; it recurred within 5 minutes of a restart.
- Setting `"reasoning": false` on the model — **does not disable thinking**; the very next turn still reported `tokens.reasoning = 1646`. The flag appears to change how opencode treats the response, not what the provider returns.

## Detection

This leaves no log line, so it has to be caught from the session DB:

```
opencode db "select id, time_created, json_extract(data,'$.tokens.output') as out,
  json_extract(data,'$.tokens.reasoning') as rea from message
  where json_extract(data,'$.role')='assistant'
    and json_extract(data,'$.finish')='stop'
    and coalesce(json_extract(data,'$.tokens.output'),0)=0" --format json
```

---

*This report was compiled and filed by Claude (Anthropic's CLI coding agent) on behalf of the affected user. The measurements and queries come from that user's own environment; wording and triage are mine.*

while waiting for `system` on prompt/command, i tried `session.instructions.entry.put` as the replacement.

that api is capped at **8kb** (`InstructionEntry.MaxValueBytes` in https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/v2/packages/schema/src/instruction-entry.ts, from #36254). over that it 413s with `InstructionEntryValueTooLargeError`. no truncate.

that limit does not make sense as a stand-in for v1 `system`.

v1 `promptAsync({ system })` took a full session system prompt. kimaki's is tens of kb: discord routing, slash commands, shell extra fields, session ids. AGENTS.md / skill files already inject large instruction text through discovery. hashing and blob storage in #36254 already handle arbitrary json values. an 8kb wall only on the public PUT is an artificial client limit, not a storage one.

please remove `MaxValueBytes` (or raise it to something that can actually hold a session system prompt). otherwise `entry.put` cannot replace `system`, and every harness has to invent a side channel (file, sqlite, plugin hook) to do what v1 did in one field.

still want `system` / `noReply` on `session.prompt` and `session.command` as the real fix. dropping the 8kb cap is the workaround so `entry.put` after `session.create` can hold the same text until then.

The cellular case @bertshim raises is the one I ended up building for, so: a data point, not a suggestion.

Disclosure first — I maintain Lauther (lauther.app), so treat this as a maker's words. It is precisely the tradeoff this issue scopes out: a cloud relay, so it works on cellular with no tailnet, and correspondingly it is not local-first and not self-hostable. If the LAN/QR version lands it covers the next-room case and this is irrelevant. I'm writing because the "away from the network entirely" half looks like it stays open either way.

Two things that mattered more than I expected, in case they save anyone the same iteration:

Silence must not read as yes. The blocking call returns three outcomes rather than two — APPROVED, DENIED, and NO ANSWER — and the tool description tells the model in words that a timeout means stop, do not retry, do not find another way. Two states plus a timeout is the easy design, and it quietly turns "I was in a tunnel" into consent.

One pending action should be one notification. On the muting point: the relay long-polls for 25 seconds at a time, and past that it re-asks about the same pending request instead of sending a new one. A ten-minute wait is one question on the phone, not one every half minute. That does not fix an agent that asks about everything — nothing downstream can — but it stops the waiting itself from generating the noise.

On what the approval screen shows: agreed this decides the whole thing. A short question plus a separate details blob for the command or diff is what made it readable on a lock screen instead of a blind tap.

Happy to go into how the relay half works if it's useful while you scope this, and equally happy for it to be irrelevant if opencode stays local-only.

**New occurrence — 2026-09-10, same channel/model, new variant (tool-call argument leaked into text)**

We hit this again today on `opencode-go` + `qwen3.7-plus`, and this occurrence exposes detail that the original report could only infer.

**Call record** (client log, timestamps GMT+8):

```
2026-09-10 23:12:52  API call #11: model=qwen3.7-plus provider=opencode-go in=55212 out=819 latency=9.2s
2026-09-10 23:12:52  Turn ended: reason=text_response(finish_reason=stop) response_len=2498
```

Client was Hermes 0.21.1 — a build that sends `x-opencode-session` on main and auxiliary OpenCode requests (per PR #101864). So the missing-session-header hypothesis raised in the original report can be ruled out for this occurrence: the request was correctly session-tagged and still corrupted.

**What the model was doing:** generating a ~2.5 KB `write_file` tool-call argument (a shell script). The expected response shape is `blocks=[thinking, tool_use]` with `stop_reason=tool_use`.

**What came back instead:** `finish_reason=stop`, **no** `tool_calls`, and **no error anywhere**.

- `reasoning` field: `"...\n"` — byte-for-byte the same debris signature as in the original report's Sample C
- `content`: 2497 chars, starting mid-stream, ending with an orphaned `</parameter>`

Trimmed sample (no local paths or credentials are present in this text; one auth header redacted):

```
...
",
            "role": "user"
        }
    ],
    "max_tokens": 2048,
    "stream": True,
    "stream_options": {"include_usage": True}
}
REQ

t0=$(date +%s.%N)
first_reasoning=""
...
done < <(curl -sS -N -X POST "$BASE/chat/completions" \
    -H "User-Agent: <redacted>" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer [redacted]" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    --data @/tmp/test_req.json)

...
echo "===== SUMMARY ====="
echo "Date: $(date)"

</parameter>
```

**Why this is a sharper view of the same bug.** The swallowed head is not arbitrary text — it is the **opening structural markup of the tool call**. The response we should have received began with `<function_calls><invoke name="write_file"><parameter name="path">…</parameter><parameter name="content">`; what survived starts *inside* the argument body and still carries the closing `</parameter>`. In the original report the swallowed head was a code-fence opener; here it is the tool-call opener. Same mechanism, clearer film — consistent with a think-block/reasoning-split path that occasionally takes the first chunk of content with it.

**Client-side parsing is excluded.** Hermes' anthropic transport parses structured content blocks (`text` / `thinking` / `tool_use`) and does not interpret XML at all; there is no parse warning in the client log for this turn. A control probe against the same endpoint and model returns `blocks=['thinking','tool_use']`, `stop_reason='tool_use'`, and **no XML anywhere in the text**. So `</parameter>` appearing in the message body means the text block handed to the client was already malformed upstream.

**Reproduction attempt:** we re-ran the same trigger (long tool-call argument, anthropic wire, same endpoint) 6 times — 0/6 recurrences, consistent with the intermittent rate described in the original report.

**Impact, worth underlining:** this failure mode is *silent*. `finish_reason=stop` with no error means an agent client stores it as a normal reply; when it lands on a tool call, the tool is never invoked and the step is silently dropped. That is how it was caught here — a run that should have written a test script simply produced text instead.

> 
> “enabled” means the default value is “ask” or is “deny” set? There’s a subtlety here: in fully automatic operation (if you run `opencode --auto`), “ask” turns into “allow”.
> 
> Furthermore, as far as I know, subagents or specific agents can use their own permission scheme, i.e., when calling a subagent, it may turn out that doom_loop is disabled. Perhaps the problem isn’t the lack of a loop protection, but the fact that subagents don’t use it. It’s interesting to check; perhaps I’ll try tomorrow.

It was set to "ask", but I tried "deny" as well and it failed. I fixed it with a custom plugin, but obviously that's just to fix my case here. It could also be an interaction with openchamber (which I'm well aware wouldn't be on opencode at that point) but I was unable to verify that since the bypassing happens basically randomly. I can confirm I have only ever seen this with subagents, and it doesn't matter if they're background or not. The entire sequence itself is very odd in that the times I saw it happen were essentially success loops. Subagent would read a file, get what it was looking for, and do the exact same read on the exact same lines over and over again until it auto-compacted and fixed itself. It consumed tokens the entire time, so the data was being consumed.

Custom plugin I wrote essentially just does this:
Track repeated tool results per child, grouped by the same resource/call family rather than just identical arguments. That lets it catch things like different shell commands repeatedly reading the same file and returning the same content.
If a child gets an already-seen result, append a recovery warning telling it to change approach. It gets 5 recovery attempts.
If it makes genuine progress, reset the incident.
After recovery 5/5, an exact repeat is blocked before execution and the child session is aborted.
If it changes the arguments enough to avoid that pre-execution check but still gets the same already-seen result from the same resource, abort it immediately afterward.
Abort the child through session.abort() rather than throwing from the hook, so the plugin itself doesn’t break the session/plugin chain.
Store a diagnostic when killing the child, then use experimental.chat.messages.transform to replace the generic parent-facing "Task cancelled" error with a useful report explaining which tool/resource looped and why the child was terminated.

That entirely fixed it for me. The bug has happened twice since then, both times with glm-5.3-flash (which itself might just be misaligned on tool use and that's the root cause, idk), but plugin stepped in, parent resumed subagent thread, and it went back to normal work.

Based on my search, I found one potentially related PR:

**Related PR:**
- **[fix(session): answer queued prompts after a stopped turn](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/pull/48339)** (PR #48339)

Correcting the measurements in the issue body — the reuse comparison was computed unfairly and overstates the gap.

I computed reuse as `cache_read / (uncached_input + cache_read)`. That omits `cache_creation_input_tokens`, which is part of the prompt. Anthropic reports it; the OpenAI-family paths report zero, because automatic prefix caching has no separately reported write.

Over the last 7 days on my setup:

| model | cache write / turn | reuse without write | reuse with write |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| claude-sonnet-5 | 5,900 | 100.0% | 97.4% |
| claude-opus-5 | 8,243 | 100.0% | 97.4% |
| claude-fable-5-1 | 10,406 | 100.0% | 96.8% |
| gpt-6-astra | 0 | 92.0% | 92.0% |
| gpt-5.6-luna | 0 | 92.5% | 92.5% |

So the honest comparison is **97.4% vs 92.0%**, not 100.0% vs 92.1%. The write volume is the cost of maintaining the moving breakpoint, and it belongs in the denominator.

The second correction matters more. I said Anthropic showed no sustained collapse. It does. Scanning for runs of three or more consecutive turns under 25% reuse, with cache reads flat while the prompt grows, and excluding runs explained by a deliberate context rewrite:

| model | turns | sustained-collapse rate |
|---|---:|---:|
| claude-opus-5 | 4,374 | 0.43% |
| gpt-6-astra | 1,745 | 2.12% |
| claude-sonnet-5 | 18,353 | 0.00% |

Five such runs on `claude-opus-5` in 7 days, ~6.1M tokens. Explicit breakpoints reduce sustained collapse by roughly 5x here; they do not prevent it.

What I still stand behind is the code claim, which is independent of the measurements: `applyCaching()` is reached only for Anthropic-family models, the native `openai` provider never gets a breakpoint, and `promptCacheBreakpoint` has no callers in the repository despite both converters supporting it.

For anyone weighing #48267 — the change is still worth making, but the expected gain is closer to 5 points of reuse than 8, and it will not eliminate the plateau failure mode on its own. I have not established what sustains a plateau once it starts; reads stay pinned at a constant for many turns even when the array is only being appended to, and that is unexplained on both families.

Heads up for review: I've corrected the measurements motivating this in anomalyco/opencode#48246.

The reuse gap is smaller than I first reported — 97.4% vs 92.0%, not 100.0% vs 92.1% — because the original figure omitted cache-creation tokens from the denominator. And Anthropic-family models are not immune to the sustained-collapse pattern, at roughly a fifth the rate rather than zero.

The code claim is unchanged. This is still worth doing; the expected gain is just smaller than the issue originally implied, and it won't eliminate the plateau failure mode by itself.

I'd like to work on this.

I traced the v2 request path to understand how a single prompt can drain a per-request (legacy) quota. What I found so far:

- One user prompt fans out into many provider requests: each agent-loop step is its own `llm.stream` call (one request per step/tool-call round), plus separate `title` and `compaction` requests (`SessionRequestKind = "primary" | "compaction" | "title" | "generate"` in `packages/plugin/src/effect/session.ts`).
- Copilot requests are tagged by origin in `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/github-copilot.ts`: `X-Interaction-Type` maps the request kind (`conversation-agent`, `conversation-background`, `conversation-compaction`, `conversation-subagent`) and `x-initiator` is set to `agent` for anything that is not a fresh user turn (`requestMetadata` / `applyHeaders`).
- Retries are bounded (`RETRY_AFTER_MAX = 15 minutes` in `packages/core/src/session/runner/retry.ts`), so an unbounded retry storm is not the likely cause on its own.

So the working hypothesis is that per-request plans are being billed per provider call rather than per user turn — every step, retry, title, and compaction request consumes a request from the monthly bucket. A single multi-step prompt with tool calls can therefore consume dozens of requests, which matches "used all my requests in a single session".

I plan to:
1. Instrument/verify the exact provider request count per user prompt (primary steps + title + compaction) for a legacy per-request Copilot account.
2. Check whether v2 is missing the request-counting signal that v1 used (or whether the agent-loop step requests should be coalesced/attributed differently for per-request plans).
3. Propose the smallest fix that preserves the existing design, with a regression test.

If maintainers already know the intended accounting for legacy per-request plans, pointers are welcome. Otherwise I'll start with the request-count trace and report back before changing behavior.

I recommend hiding compaction-owned parts and synthetic continuation prompts in both --format json and the default text mode. They are internal session mechanics, not user-visible assistant output; exposing them in plain text is the same leak with a less structured consumer. The shared event loop already has one owner-message filter, so applying it to both modes avoids divergent behavior without changing the JSONL schema. Please keep ordinary assistant text (and explicitly requested reasoning) unchanged, and add one default-text regression alongside the JSONL test.

I encountered this same issue while running `opencode` in a Ubuntu 24.04 Docker container (but the markdown rendering worked running outside the container, also Ubuntu 24.04).

The root issue was that I had a bind mount for `~/.local/share/opencode`, but not for `~/.local/share/opentui`, so when docker starts the container the directories `~/local/` and `~/.local/share/` were owned by `root`, so when opencode attempted to create the `~/.local/share/opentui/` directory for tree-sitter wasm files it just failed with EPERM (Permission Denied), which caused the rendering to fail. In my case this was simply fixed by adding the missing mount for `~/.local/share/opentui`.

The reason rendering seems to work while the response is being streamed in is likely due to it using `marked` (pure JS) at that time, but then when the response is finished it only uses `tree-sitter` (which was failing).

Something similar is probably happening in @Cesarucho case when switching `/themes`.

Could likely be fixed by either using `marked` as a real fallback in case `tree-sitter` fails, or just make the `tree-sitter` error visible to the user so they can diagnose and fix the issue themselves.

One safety correction to the blanket `DELETE FROM event WHERE type IN (...)` recovery recipe above: non-empty `message` and `part` projection tables do not by themselves make partial event deletion replay-safe. `replayAll` requires contiguous aggregate sequence numbers, so deleting selected event types from a surviving aggregate can leave sequence holes and make later replay/sync diverge. A backup and `VACUUM` protect file recovery and reclaim pages, but they do not restore that event-level invariant.

#41711 is now rebased onto current `dev` and proposes a conservative built-in path for the existing V1 snapshot stock:

- Analyze is read-only and runs against a consistent temporary database snapshot.
- Only superseded `message.updated.1` and `message.part.updated.1` rows are considered.
- The retained latest snapshot must match the current projection.
- Apply replaces eligible old payloads with small durable checkpoint markers while preserving each event ID and aggregate sequence position; it does not blanket-delete `session.updated.1`.
- Workspace/sync-owned aggregates are report-only because the protocol has no checkpoint-marker negotiation yet.
- The Settings Storage Compact action creates and verifies a backup before rewriting; Vacuum is a separate confirmed, backup-first operation for reclaiming physical file space.
- A process-wide maintenance gate drains active session work and returns 503 for new mutations during destructive maintenance instead of relying on users to race a live server manually.

The current revision passed 220 targeted tests with one expected skip, the 8/8 storage HttpApi exercise, generated-artifact checks, and workspace typecheck 30/30. This is still an unmerged PR, not release recovery guidance, but its sequence-preserving model is the important distinction from deleting selected rows directly.
